headline_insight: Households including a person with disability were significantly more likely to have experienced an insured event (26.9% vs 16.1%, n=453 vs 1,499) yet less likely to have submitted a claim (36.1% vs 45.2%), and were roughly twice as likely to have coped by drawing down savings (10.1% vs 5.6%), borrowing (10.9% vs 6.2%) or selling assets and livestock (4.0% vs 1.5%) "paragraphs
paragraphs: The clearest and most robust disability finding in the 2026 survey is one of exposure, not attitude. Among the 453 PWD-inclusive households and 1,499 non-PWD households who answered, 26.9% of PWD households had experienced an insured event compared with 16.1% of non-PWD households \u2013 a 10.9 percentage point gap that remains significant after adjustment for multiple comparisons. That higher shock exposure is mirrored in coping behaviour: PWD households were significantly more likely to have used savings (10.1% vs 5.6%), borrowed money (10.9% vs 6.2%) and sold assets or livestock (4.0% vs 1.5%). These are three separately significant indicators pointing the same direction, and together they describe a client segment absorbing more shocks with more erosive coping strategies.

What makes this consequential for product design is that the higher exposure does not translate into higher claiming. Of those who experienced an event, 36.1% of PWD households submitted a claim against 45.2% of non-PWD households (a 9.2 point gap, not statistically significant after adjustment, so directional). The stated reasons differ in an important way: PWD non-claimants were considerably less likely than others to say they did not know how to file (23.1% vs 38.6%) and considerably more likely to say they were not covered at the time (42.3% vs 29.5%) \u2013 though both sit on small bases (n=78 and n=132) and should be read as illustrative. Where PWD clients did claim, 63.6% reported claim challenges versus 52.3% of others, again on a small base (n=44 vs 109). The pattern suggests the binding constraint for this segment is coverage continuity and claims accompaniment, not basic literacy about the product.

Health insurance outcomes reinforce this. PWD households were significantly less likely to report that out-of-pocket costs were much lower after insurance (9.0% vs 14.8%) and significantly more likely to report no difference at all (30.0% vs 19.8%); 47.1% said insurance had not made accessing medical care easier, against 41.0% of non-PWD households (not significant after adjustment). Yet understanding of coverage and of the claims process is statistically indistinguishable between the two groups, as is confidence in payout (72.7% vs 70.7% very confident) and the judgement that insurance is worth the cost (73.3% in both groups). The divergence is therefore not one between quant and qual \u2013 no qualitative material was available for this section, and no client voice can be quoted here \u2013 but an internal one within the quantitative data: PWD clients value and trust the product as much as anyone, while realising measurably less financial protection from it. No external benchmark data is available for any of these disability indicators.

For programming, three implications follow. First, the coverage-gap finding argues for reviewing enrolment continuity and renewal touchpoints for PWD-inclusive households, since the most-cited reason for not claiming was being uncovered at the time of the shock. Second, 63.7% of PWD clients prefer claims via an MFI officer collecting documents and 63.5% rate in-person explanation from staff as effective \u2013 both marginally above non-PWD clients \u2013 while digital channels are negligible (1.0% smartphone app, 0.8% e-mail); assisted, human-mediated claims handling should be treated as an accessibility requirement rather than a legacy cost. Third, PWD clients on Enhanced Credit Life rated the additional benefits \"very valuable\" at 79.1% versus 59.9% (n=43, directional only, and not significant after adjustment), suggesting real appetite for bundled protection in a segment that is simultaneously less likely to know that medical cost support is already included (8.6% vs 14.1%, significant). Closing that awareness gap is a low-cost first move.
